📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

Industry observers note that it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” states Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”.

Industry observers note that but when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin states. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Industry observers note that domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

In a recent development, such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, notes Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in Newly introduced York and Wisconsin.

According to recent reports, as of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

It has been revealed that measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

Sources indicate that the United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that in the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

In a recent development, during the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

In a recent development, it has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and New York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

According to recent reports, in June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy indicates.

According to recent reports, but it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

Industry observers note that it can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials declared a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, noted Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”.

According to recent reports, sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she noted they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”.

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

It has been revealed that FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the New York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

According to recent reports, without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, indicates Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”.

Starting in 2027, FDA intends to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, notes Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to promptly contain outbreaks.

“We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”.

It has been revealed that when the WHO unveiled in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, notes the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered.

As cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Industry observers note that before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, claims infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

In a recent development, kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

It has been revealed that by September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of fresh Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli claims.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli states. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

In a recent development, nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

According to recent reports, conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli claims.

Recent findings suggest that the M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

It has been revealed that more than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

According to recent reports, the United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” says Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”.

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”.

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the Newly introduced York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm indicates. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”.

According to recent reports, the outbreak, which ended July 2, was rapidly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm claims. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”.

The international collaboration had some successes, indicates virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in Upcoming York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

It has been revealed that hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

In a recent development, “The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a latest one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

Recent findings suggest that “We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become crucial,” Palacios states. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”.

Industry News: Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.
  • For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step.
  • It has been revealed that researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

It has been revealed that researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

Recent findings suggest that during angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

Recent findings suggest that for the upcoming analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

In a recent development, earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

“When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” remarked Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

Industry observers note that “We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”.

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a newly introduced randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

Sources indicate that the research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala mentioned considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

In a recent development, reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488.

Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find Newly introduced Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.
  • In a recent development, A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years.
  • Sources indicate that for example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

In a recent development, A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a latest Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

Sources indicate that for example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

Industry observers note that the method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

The approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” states Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very vital in treatment decisions.”.

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” indicates Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”.

Recent findings suggest that the risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292.

Scientists Develop New Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery.
  • Recent findings suggest that developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors.
  • Sources indicate that cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. In preclinical testing, the experimental nanomaterial produced approximately 80 percent more new bone than a control material after eight weeks.

Recent findings suggest that developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors. Researchers hope the approach could eventually allow children to receive treatment years earlier than is typically possible today.

Sources indicate that cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy. Correcting the resulting jawbone defects is among the most challenging aspects of treatment, with potential consequences for eating, breathing, speech, and social development.

“One of the biggest challenges for children born with cleft lip and palate is repairing the bone defect in the jaw,” said lead researcher Associate Professor Chun Xu, a Sydney Horizon Fellow in the University of Sydney’s Faculty of Medicine and Health.

“While some children with minor defects are treated as infants, many patients need to wait until they are around 10 to 12 years old before surgeons can take bone from another part of the body and graft it into the defect.

“That means many kids live with difficulties for years. It can affect their breathing, eating and speech. Most heartbreaking of all, it can have a huge impact on their confidence and social development.”.

In a recent development, more than four million bone repair procedures are performed worldwide annually. Many current treatments rely on bone harvested from the patient or animal-derived materials that primarily provide structural support. The upcoming approach instead aims to stimulate the formation of living bone using a biodegradable calcium-aluminosilicate nanomaterial.

The material activates a naturally occurring growth factor called latent Transforming Growth Factor β1 (TGF-β1). This protein normally exists in an inactive form until biological signals trigger its activity. Once activated, it helps recruit stem cells to the damaged area and encourages their development into bone-producing cells. As new tissue forms, the biodegradable material is gradually replaced by the patient’s own bone.

“The material activates dormant repair signals in the body, triggering a cascade of healing processes that attract bone-forming stem cells and stimulate new bone growth,” Xu explained.

“Our body already contains many of the signals needed for tissue repair,” Associate Professor Xu mentioned.

“We’ve developed a material that can help activate those signals at the right place and time. Instead of supplying external growth factors, we’re encouraging the body to use its own healing potential.”.

In a recent development, the study, published in ACS Nano, found that the material activated the body’s latent bone repair growth factor at approximately 10 times the level achieved using conventional methods. It also promoted blood clotting within about 30 seconds, which could help stabilize an injury during the earliest stages of healing.

According to the researchers, this is the first demonstration of a single nanomaterial platform capable of combining rapid blood clotting, activation of naturally occurring growth factors, recruitment of bone-forming stem cells, and enhanced bone regeneration. The findings come from a preclinical bone model, however, and further testing is necessary to determine whether the material can be used safely and effectively in humans.

Xu and his colleagues envision a future in which bone defects can be repaired earlier in childhood, potentially reducing the need to remove healthy bone from elsewhere in the body.

“Our long-term goal is to develop materials that help the body regenerate bone naturally and reduce the need for these invasive and painful procedures. We hope this could allow treatment much earlier than is possible today.”.

The researchers are also investigating whether the nanomaterial could be incorporated into personalized 3D-printed scaffolds designed to fit an individual’s bone defect. Beyond cleft lip and palate, potential applications include repairing bone damaged by traumatic injuries, tooth loss, and other conditions involving difficult-to-heal defects.

“Every patient is different, and every bone defect is different,” Xu remarked.

“In the future, we hope to combine these materials with advanced 3D-printing technologies so treatments can be tailored to the specific needs of each patient.”.

The technology remains at the preclinical stage, with additional research required before human trials can begin.

Industry observers note that reference: “Multifunctional Mesoporous Calcium-Aluminosilicate Nanoparticles Enable Heterogeneous Activation of Endogenous Transforming Growth Factor β1 and Rapid Hemostasis for Bone Repair” by Chun Xu, Qingxuan Chen, Hang Chen, Aoni Xu, Juan Wen, Yiwei Li, Huan Dai, Siyuan Liu, Dan Cheng, Yaping Song, Bing Sun, Jie Tang, Jie Fan, Chang Lei and Chengzhong Yu, 15 September 2026, ACS Nano. DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c05126.

According to recent reports, the authors acknowledge the funding support from Australian Research Council, National Health and Medical Research Council and the University of Sydney. A provisional patent application related to the findings reported in this manuscript has been filed by the University of Sydney and the University of Queensland. The application covers calcium-aluminosilicate mesoporous nanoparticles and their use for bone repair, as described in the paper (Provisional Patent Application No. 2026903515).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.

At the time, “one of the significant questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” claims Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”.

Recent findings suggest that one key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s important for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.

Pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.

Recent findings suggest that “As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals says. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”.

In a recent development, experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.

Sources indicate that generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It has been revealed that as a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

Sources indicate that A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you initiative to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

In a recent development, they’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, says Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

In a recent development, instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

According to recent reports, these systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”.

It has been revealed that yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” says Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Recent findings suggest that both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

Some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that concern without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

It has been revealed that “Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”.

Some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

According to recent reports, “When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Recent findings suggest that smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

Does the Sun Have a Secret Companion? A Controversial Theory Could Explain Earth’s Mass Extinctions

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.
  • According to recent reports, scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud.
  • Industry observers note that richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.

According to recent reports, scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud. This vast, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies is thought to contain trillions of objects and extend as far as 1.6 light-years from the Sun.

Industry observers note that richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system. In addition to gravitational disturbances caused by passing stars, he suggests that a low-mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) could periodically redirect comets toward the Sun. Under this hypothesis, Nemesis and the Sun orbit a shared center of gravity.

According to Muller, Nemesis follows a slightly elongated orbit that periodically brings it into regions of the Oort Cloud, where its gravity could disrupt the paths of billions of comets.

Recent findings suggest that muller explained in a phone interview that these encounters could trigger comet showers lasting roughly a million years. The greatest number of comets would be redirected into the inner solar system when Nemesis passes through the cloud’s densest regions.

The proposed Nemesis star is not related to the hypothetical Planet X. It also differs from unrelated stars that occasionally pass near the solar system and gravitationally disturb the Oort Cloud, potentially sending numerous comets inward.

Unlike these unpredictable stellar encounters, the Nemesis hypothesis proposes a recurring cycle. Muller believes this mechanism could explain a pattern of impacts on Earth spanning approximately 250 million years.

Recent findings suggest that muller points to a 1982 study published in the journal Science by paleontologists David Raup and Jack Sepkoski. The researchers compiled an extensive record of marine extinctions that, according to Muller, revealed a striking pattern of extinction events occurring roughly every 26 million years.

Sources indicate that the challenge was to come up with an explanation, says Muller. “Well, maybe there’s a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth,” he says.

It’s an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn’t sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, claims Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of France’s Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email.

Planetesimals that originated in our Sun’s planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun’s birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he says.

Industry observers note that many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because it’s moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesn’t show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be massive enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means it’s probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, indicates Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

In a recent development, yet the evidence that it’s an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that’s what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, remarked in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, “You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?”.

He responded, “Sure, we couldn’t tell the difference.”.

In a recent development, the best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long-period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, indicates Muller.

The bad news is that if it’s out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie coplanar with most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, indicates Muller.

References: “Dynamical Population of Comet Reservoirs” by Nathan A. Kaib and Kathryn Volk, May 30, 2022, arXiv. DOI: 2206.00010.

“Measurement of the lunar impact record for the past 3.5 b.y. and implications for the Nemesis theory” by Richard A. Muller, 01 January 2002, Geological Society of America DOI: 10.1130/0-8137-2356-6.659.

Recent findings suggest that “Mass Extinctions in the Marine Fossil Record” by David M. Raup and J. John Sepkoski, Jr., 19 March 1982, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.215.4539.1501.

#77314. Industry News: NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

Industry News: NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks.
  • The spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’.
  • “Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

The spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”.

Navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

It has been revealed that didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

According to recent reports, these conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

In a recent development, rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

Sources indicate that the technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Industry observers note that hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

During this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

In a recent development, supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

It has been revealed that that day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

The experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

In a recent development, however, the results also raised vital questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

Industry observers note that the spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an key role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

#77310. An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a New Era of Optical Computing

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)

An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a New Era of Optical Computing

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.
  • Industry observers note that for decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work.
  • The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.

Industry observers note that for decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work. Now, researchers in South Africa have discovered that a magnetic field can also affect light when it points sideways across a fiber, challenging an assumption that has guided optical engineering for more than 50 years.

The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them. It may also offer a new way to control light for optical computing.

It has been revealed that MSc student Mohammed Raiyan Sharif and Professor Mitchell Cox at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg demonstrated the previously overlooked interaction, known as the transverse Faraday effect. Their research was conducted at the Wits Optical Communication (OC) Lab in the university’s School of Electrical and Information Engineering.

Industry observers note that optical fibers carry internet signals through thin strands of glass, but they can also detect magnetic fields. This sensing ability relies on the Faraday effect, first observed by Michael Faraday in glass in 1845. When a magnetic field points along the direction light travels, it slightly rotates the light’s polarization, or the direction in which its electric field oscillates. Measuring that rotation can reveal the strength of the magnetic field and the electrical current producing it.

A sideways magnetic field was not expected to produce the same effect. To investigate, Sharif and Cox placed strong magnets beside a stationary multimode optical fiber without touching it, then watched the light emerging from the other end.

Multimode fibers have relatively wide glass cores that allow light to travel along many different paths, repeatedly reflecting off the core’s mirror-like boundary. At the output, the overlapping waves create a pattern of bright and dark spots called speckle, similar to the shifting patterns inside a kaleidoscope.

Recent findings suggest that as the researchers rearranged the magnets, a camera recorded changes in that pattern. The sideways magnetic field was somehow altering the light’s behavior inside the fiber.

“It wasn’t hard to 3D print a rig to test our intuition. Working out the theory for what we were seeing was the challenging part,” says Sharif. “The key was to return to the underlying equations and question assumptions that are usually taken for granted in fiber optics.”.

Industry observers note that the explanation involved a small part of the light wave that a widely used mathematical shortcut ignores. Known as the weak-guidance approximation, this approach assumes that light’s electric field oscillates almost entirely across the fiber, leaving out a tiny component that oscillates along its length.

The approximation works extremely well when the fiber’s core and surrounding glass have similar refractive indices, which describe how strongly a material slows light. However, Sharif and Cox tested step-index fibers, where the refractive index changes abruptly at the core’s boundary rather than gradually, as it does in graded-index fibers.

When that difference is large, the normally neglected longitudinal component becomes significant near the core’s edge. By including it in their equations, the researchers showed that a sideways magnetic field transfers some of the light’s transverse oscillation into the longitudinal component. This changes how light reflects inside the fiber and, ultimately, the speckle pattern it produces.

It has been revealed that the team also distinguished the new interaction from the Cotton-Mouton effect, another response to sideways magnetic fields. The Cotton-Mouton effect increases with the square of the magnetic field’s strength, while the transverse Faraday effect increases in direct proportion to it.

Their measurements confirmed four predictions. The effect disappeared without a sufficiently strong step in refractive index, became stronger when light entered at steeper angles, occurred for only one polarization relative to the magnetic field, and varied with wavelength in the same way as the conventional Faraday effect.

With a magnetic field of 0.24 tesla, roughly the strength found close to a powerful neodymium magnet, light polarized across the field produced a speckle pattern only about 84% similar to the original.

“What is surprising is finding an overlooked, useful interaction in such a familiar technology,” states Cox. “It’s quite exciting that there is always something new to learn or discover, and often these things are right under our noses, hidden in the assumptions we have made for decades.”.

In a recent development, one possible application is monitoring electrical currents with fibers laid alongside cables, including those buried in trenches. However, magnetic fields near most cables are much weaker than those used in the experiment, so the sensitivity of a practical sensor remains uncertain.

The researchers also envision replacing permanent magnets with electrical coils, allowing currents to control the patterns of light traveling through a fiber.

“Besides sensing, I think that being able to control different modes (patterns of light) inside the fiber electrically could unlock a latest way to do optical computing,” notes Cox. “We can model the way light gets distorted when it propagates through fibers, frosted glass windows, or even the atmosphere. If we change our perspective on those models, we can actually use light to do mathematical computations for us, for free.”.

Reference: “Transverse Faraday effect in multimode fibers” by Mohammed R. Sharif and Mitchell A. Cox, 30 September 2026, Optics Letters. DOI: 10.1364/OL.611078.

The research was supported by the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the National Research Foundation (NRF).

Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • According to recent reports, for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter.
  • In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Recent findings suggest that now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

It has been revealed that instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Massive Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

According to recent reports, they’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Upcoming Once-Daily Pill Slashes Bad Cholesterol by Nearly 65% in Clinical Trial

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.
  • It has been revealed that high cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms.
  • A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

It has been revealed that high cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

In a recent development, enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

It has been revealed that by blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

Industry observers note that A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57.1% to 64.6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

According to recent reports, in a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

Recent findings suggest that the review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

Enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

While clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

In a recent development, reference: “Enlicitide: The First Oral PCSK9i for Lowering Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol” by Rachel C. Lucas, Mia E. Lussier, Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi and Taylor M. Clark, 14 October 2026, Annals of Pharmacotherapy. DOI: 10.1177/10600280261494015.
