#77304. A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (874 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.
  • A upcoming review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.
  • The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.

A upcoming review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

According to recent reports, treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants, so it’s vital this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

According to recent reports, studies of real-world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The upcoming review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

It has been revealed that the findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

According to recent reports, the findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

Recent findings suggest that this means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six studies followed participants for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

According to recent reports, importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

It has been revealed that continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects, and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing, or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.

#77302. Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1262 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

It has been revealed that after release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

The study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin said.

According to recent reports, A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

Recent findings suggest that the team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

The release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

According to recent reports, homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Industry observers note that eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

According to recent reports, the release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

Two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

It has been revealed that some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

None of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

The authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

On the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

The animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

This balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

Industry observers note that the burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

The researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

The tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

Twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

Every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

Two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

Industry observers note that the authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira remarked the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

📅 11 Oct 2021 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter will be here before you know it.
  • Industry observers note that of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers.
  • Recent findings suggest that they also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association states it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart problems, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Industry observers note that of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

Recent findings suggest that they also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

Ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

In a recent development, we leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

Sources indicate that with a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it debuts snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

It has been revealed that though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

In a recent development, if you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Industry observers note that ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was promptly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

It has been revealed that being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

It has been revealed that along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

In a recent development, with its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

Sources indicate that the two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For massive jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Recent findings suggest that much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

Recent findings suggest that for an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

In a recent development, electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Recent findings suggest that similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

Cerebral Palsy May Not Be What Scientists Thought It Was

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that fresh research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP).
  • Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics, the research also proposes a different way to classify CP.
  • Cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fresh research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP). Of 515 genes previously linked to the condition, only 89 demonstrated a statistically significant association in a new study, suggesting that many proposed genetic connections still lack sufficient evidence.

Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics, the research also proposes a different way to classify CP. Rather than treating it as a single disorder, the scientists suggest it may be better understood as a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions.

Cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually. It has traditionally been associated with complications around birth, including premature delivery and temporary oxygen deprivation. However, genetic research over the past decade has increasingly pointed to inherited or newly occurring genetic variants as potential contributors. Unlike progressive neurological diseases, CP does not worsen over time, and rehabilitation and physical therapy can improve symptoms.

“There has been a lack of consensus on the definition of cerebral palsy and on the role of genetics in disease pathogenesis, leading to substantial variability in whether a child is diagnosed with CP,” indicates corresponding author Peter Robinson of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine and the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité.

“We have developed a paradigm that considers CP to be a phenotypic trait rather than a precise disease diagnosis. A better understanding of specific genetic variants has the potential to improve our understanding of the biology of the disease.”.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the genetic basis of CP, the researchers evaluated evidence from 21 previously published studies involving 5,440 people diagnosed with the condition. These studies had identified potentially causal variants across hundreds of genes, but the new statistical analysis found convincing evidence of association for only a fraction of them.

Sources indicate that “We decided to do this study because there has been no accepted statistical method to determine if a disease-associated gene is truly linked to CP,” notes first author Adam Arterbery of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine. “We discovered it was extremely difficult to find statistical evidence of causality for many of the genetic variants previously linked to CP.”.

The team also performed whole-genome sequencing on 460 children from 453 families receiving care at Shriners Children’s hospitals across the United States. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variants were identified in 70 families, spanning 60 genes. However, just 16 of those genes overlapped with the genes supported by statistically significant evidence in the analysis of earlier studies.

It has been revealed that the researchers emphasize that their findings do not disprove connections between CP and the remaining genes. Instead, the available data are insufficient to establish those associations with statistical confidence. They propose viewing CP as a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences, rather than a single disease with a common biological origin.

“This framework could improve interpretation of genomic testing, help identify children who may warrant closer CP surveillance or specialist referral, and potentially identify genetic conditions requiring disease-specific management,” Robinson says. “But clinical utility and patient benefit will absolutely need validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.”.

It has been revealed that future studies will focus on larger patient populations, prospective evaluations of clinical benefits and costs, and better access to genomic and medical data. “We hope our study will stimulate discussion about CP terminology, gene-disease associations, and variant interpretation,” Arterbery says. “The most productive response will be further validation and development of better genotype-phenotype evidence rather than treating the findings as a definitive list of CP genes.”.

Reference: “A phenotypic paradigm for cerebral palsy genetics” by Adam S. Arterbery, Michael A. Gargano, Anita Bagley, Jagadish Chandrabose Sundaramurthi, Lauren Rekerle, Thania Ordaz-Robles, Daniel Danis, Adam S.L. Graefe, Ana L. Arenas-Díaz, Jeremy P. Breaking: Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.
  • Industry observers note that some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs.
  • Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.

Industry observers note that some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs. Yet roughly half its living species arose within the past six million years, as mountains rose and landscapes changed.

Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.

The findings draw on decades of work identifying ferns and establishing where they grow. That groundwork made it possible to investigate how the group spread and diversified.

“We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest,” stated senior author Hanna Tuomisto, a professor of ecology.

“In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 new Danaea species previously unknown to science, and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus.”.

“We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team combined DNA evidence from 78 species with 2,289 verified records of where the ferns grow. These records helped reconstruct where ancestral ferns probably lived and the elevations they occupied.

The genetic analysis included 11 species that had not yet been formally described.

The researchers’ preferred estimate suggests that the Danaea lineage split from the lineage of its closest living relatives about 128 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

The common ancestor of its surviving species lived much later, around 53 million years ago. The researchers traced that ancestor to Amazonia.

It has been revealed that but an ancient lineage need not consist of ancient species. About half of today’s Danaea species originated during the past six million years.

This complicates a familiar explanation for tropical richness: favorable conditions allowed species to accumulate over immense stretches of time.

Persistence mattered, but the landscape also kept changing, creating opportunities for fresh species.

Fern diversity generally reaches its greatest heights in tropical mountain forests. Danaea follows a different pattern: Amazonia has consistently held its largest pool of species in the reconstruction.

Industry observers note that “Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes – plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor,” said lead author Venni Keskiniva, a postdoctoral researcher at Turku.

“These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests.”.

Where a plant lives within a forest may therefore help explain where its group becomes most diverse. Findings from one fern group cannot automatically describe them all.

Industry observers note that the Andes still played an crucial role. Although Amazonia contained more species, the mountains became the leading source of dispersal to other regions.

It has been revealed that mountain formation affected far more than the slopes themselves. As the Andes rose, they changed rainfall patterns along with the soils developing across neighboring lowlands.

Sources indicate that vast wetlands once occupied much of western Amazonia. Their drainage near the end of the Miocene opened additional land for forest plants to colonize.

The resulting western Amazonian soils were generally richer in nutrients and more variable, than soils in central Amazonia.

Those differences may have encouraged plants to specialize in different environments.

Sources indicate that the timing fits the fern history. Most latest Amazonian species arising within the past six million years appeared in western Amazonia during the last three million.

It has been revealed that fresh land in southern Central America also offered room for expansion. Arriving lineages frequently gave rise to additional species as the region’s landscapes developed.

The first mountain-adapted Danaea lineages appeared around 20 million years ago, following an intensification of Andean uplift. Several later spread into regions farther from the equator.

Their earlier move uphill may have helped them cope with the conditions they encountered there.

“As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater,” Keskiniva said.

Lineages that remained adapted to Amazonian lowlands tended to stay within that region.

The repeated sequence of mountain colonization followed by expansion suggests that climate tolerance influenced which routes were available.

According to recent reports, the mountains could both separate populations and help others reach new habitats. Their role changed as the landscape rose and different fern lineages established themselves.

Assigning dates to this history was difficult. Many relevant fossils are fragmentary, and researchers disagree about where they belong in the family tree.

In a recent development, the team compared three dating approaches, which produced substantially different ages. It favored the reconstruction most consistent with other biological and geological evidence.

Sources indicate that the dates remain estimates, and coinciding events do not establish a cause by themselves. Still, the findings connect the survival of ancient lineages with much younger episodes of diversification.

“The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale,” Keskiniva concluded.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers of Biogeography.

#77296. Scientists Discover Bizarre Deep-Sea Creature That Survives Without Most of Its Digestive System

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists Discover Bizarre Deep-Sea Creature That Survives Without Most of Its Digestive System

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer newly introduced clues about how life evolves.
  • According to recent reports, deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer newly introduced clues about how life evolves.

According to recent reports, deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments. A deep-sea mollusk living in the South China Sea contains a previously unknown cellular structure packed with bacteria, offering new clues about how animals adapt to conditions that would be inhospitable to most other species.

It has been revealed that the discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight. These environments contain abundant methane and hydrogen sulfide, which certain bacteria can use to support their metabolism. Animals such as deep-sea mussels, clams, and tubeworms have evolved close relationships with these microbes, providing them with shelter inside their cells in exchange for nutrients.

Until now, however, scientists had found no clear evidence that animals could develop specialized organelles dedicated to maintaining these bacterial partnerships.

The newly introduced research centers on Chaetoderma shenloong, also known as the Divine Dragon Glistenworm. This unusual mollusk belongs to the aplacophoran class Caudofoveata and can grow to more than 150 millimeters (nearly 6 inches) long, far larger than most of its relatives. Its distinctive characteristics earned it recognition as one of the “Top-Ten Marine Species of 2024.”.

In a recent development, researchers found that the animal spends much of its life buried tens of centimeters beneath the seafloor, in sediment rich in hydrogen sulfide and containing almost no oxygen. Understanding how it survives there led the team to examine an unexpected feature of its anatomy.

According to recent reports, using anatomical analysis, micro-computed tomography, and three-dimensional imaging, the scientists discovered that Chaetoderma shenloong has a digestive system unlike those of most mollusks. Its radula, a feeding structure commonly used by mollusks, is heavily reduced, while its midgut, hindgut, and anus have almost completely disappeared.

Industry observers note that instead, an extensive system of digestive glands occupies most of its body cavity. These glands contain enormous numbers of symbiotic bacteria that serve as the animal’s primary source of nutrients and energy.

Closer examination revealed something even more unusual inside the glands.

Recent findings suggest that the bacteria were concentrated within spherical structures measuring approximately 10 to 15 micrometers across. Each structure was enclosed by more than 20 layers of membrane and contained hundreds to thousands of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. The researchers named this structure the dracosphera, Latin for “dragon ball,” because of its beadlike shape and surrounding layers.

In a recent development, A single host cell accommodated more than 1,600 bacterial symbionts on average. The dracosphera also lacked familiar cellular components, including host nuclei and lysosomes, distinguishing it from an ordinary cell or a typical digestive compartment.

This arrangement suggests that the mollusk may have developed a specialized structure for housing and maintaining its bacterial partners, potentially representing a previously unrecognized form of cooperation between animals and microorganisms.

The scientists then investigated how this relationship might function in an environment where oxygen is so scarce.

In a recent development, genomic analyses of Chaetoderma shenloong and its symbiotic bacteria revealed that the microbes possess adaptations allowing them to maintain their metabolism with very little oxygen. The mollusk, meanwhile, lives deep in the sediment to obtain chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide that its bacterial partners can use.

That creates a difficult balance. The animal and its microbes must obtain the chemicals needed to sustain their partnership while coping with the severe shortage of oxygen in the surrounding mud.

Industry observers note that one possibility is that the dracosphera’s many membrane layers help manage how oxygen moves through the animal’s body. The researchers propose that these layers could slow oxygen diffusion, allowing limited supplies to be directed preferentially toward the mollusk’s own cells while still supporting its bacterial partners.

For now, this explanation remains a hypothesis that requires further testing.

Recent findings suggest that the team also found evidence suggesting that the dracosphera participates in nutrient exchange. Digestion-related cellular structures and signs of enzyme activity were abundant around the regions containing symbiotic bacteria. These observations suggest that the mollusk may obtain essential nutrients it cannot produce itself by breaking down some of its bacterial partners.

Beyond explaining how one unusual animal survives, the findings may offer insight into a much older biological process.

Scientists believe that mitochondria, which occur in animal and plant cells, and chloroplasts, found in plant cells, originated through ancient relationships between microorganisms and their hosts. Over evolutionary time, these partnerships gave rise to structures that became essential components of complex cells.

Industry observers note that the dracosphera does not establish that a similar evolutionary transition is occurring in Chaetoderma shenloong. However, its distinctive organization provides researchers with another example of how intimately animals and bacteria can cooperate, potentially helping scientists investigate how specialized organelles and latest cellular functions evolve.

The discovery could also have implications for understanding the broader deep-sea ecosystem.

It has been revealed that researchers identified traces of Chaetoderma shenloong at the mud volcano cold seep off Kyushu, Japan, and the Site F cold seep in the northern South China Sea. Together with previous records of large, closely related species in the Gulf of Mexico, these observations raise the possibility that animals with similar bacterial partnerships are more widely distributed across deep-sea cold seeps than currently recognized.

Recent findings suggest that such organisms may participate in the movement and transformation of methane, sulfur, and carbon within these ecosystems. Establishing their distribution and ecological contributions could help scientists better understand how life operates in parts of the ocean that remain poorly explored.

Reference: “A multilamellar organelle for chemosymbiosis in an aplacophoran mollusc adapted to anoxic cold seep sediment” by Yunlong Li, Chong Chen, Xu Liu, Menggong Li, Guoyong Yan, Haiyun Zhou, Hui Wang, Xiaoshan Zheng, Xing He, Shanshan Liu, Jian-Wen Qiu, Pei-Yuan Qian and Jin Sun, 30 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78965-0.

The work also received support from the National Key Research and Development Program of China, the Laoshan Laboratory, the Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province, the Guangzhou Laboratory and research funds from the HKSAR Government, among other sources.

#77295. Mussels that live in total darkness have cells that still keep a daily rhythm

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1134 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Mussels that live in total darkness have cells that still keep a daily rhythm

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep-sea mussels live in total darkness, yet their cells kept a roughly 24-hour rhythm in the lab, offering clues to how life keeps time without sunlight.
  • Deep in the Atlantic, a mussel called Bathymodiolus azoricus lives where no daylight reaches, and the tides, not the sun, change its surroundings on a schedule.
  • Even so, the mussel’s cells kept a daily rhythm when researchers grew them in a lab refrigerator, far from the seafloor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep-sea mussels live in total darkness, yet their cells kept a roughly 24-hour rhythm in the lab, offering clues to how life keeps time without sunlight.

Deep in the Atlantic, a mussel called Bathymodiolus azoricus lives where no daylight reaches, and the tides, not the sun, change its surroundings on a schedule.

Even so, the mussel’s cells kept a daily rhythm when researchers grew them in a lab refrigerator, far from the seafloor.

The finding suggests that genes that run daily clocks in flies and people also help keep time in animals that never see sunlight.

Audrey Mat, a researcher at the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany and the University of Vienna, grew the cells from mussels collected on the Atlantic seafloor.

Her team has kept two of those cultures alive for more than three and a half years.

The mussels come from the Lucky Strike vent field on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, south of the Azores, about 5,600 feet (1,700 meters) down. The water pressure there is about 170 times what it is at sea level.

At hydrothermal vents, seawater seeps into the seafloor, moves through the rock below and flows back out as hot, metal-rich fluid. Some of it reaches about 660°F (350°C).

It has been revealed that the mussels settle in cooler water nearby, between 39 and 48°F (4 and 9°C). The direction of the vent flow shifts with the tides, so the water around the mussels switches between vent fluid and ordinary seawater.

In a 2020 study, Mat and her colleagues reported that on the seafloor, the mussels’ behavior and gene activity followed mainly a tidal rhythm of about 12.4 hours.

A weaker daily rhythm showed up as well, though no clear day-night cycle reaches the vents.

Mussels from a shallower vent switched to a mostly daily pattern in a lab with lights on for 12 hours and off for 12 hours.

How an animal with no brain produces either rhythm has been unclear.

Lab cells are usually kept warm, close to body temperature. Mat tried something different.

“While cells in the laboratory usually thrive at 25 to 37 °C, our mussel cells grow in the fridge, at deep-sea temperatures,” remarked Mat, who first proposed the experiments.

“This technical advance is unique in the world and allows novel insights into the biology of these animals.”.

Sources indicate that the team tried cells from six tissues at three temperatures. At 77°F (25°C), fungi and other contaminants quickly took over.

Out of 63 cultures, cells from the mussel’s foot survived best. The foot is the muscular part a mussel extends from its shell.

Keeping whole mussels alive took work too.

About half of the animals collected in 2023 died within a month, likely from the stress of the trip to the surface and the flight to Vienna.

The remaining mussels lived for 13 months in an aquarium shielded from white light.

To look for a clock, the team put foot tissue from five mussels in culture and kept it in constant darkness at 39°F (4°C). Then they sampled the cells every four hours for two days.

Industry observers note that A pattern of gene activity that repeats about every 24 hours is called a circadian rhythm. Finding one is how scientists spot a clock at work.

Sources indicate that of 5,616 genes the team could track, 157 indicated a circadian pattern, about 2.8%. That’s close to the 2.5% the team found earlier in mussels on the seafloor.

So the cells kept time on their own, with no ocean and no daylight around them.

Across 10,000 reshuffles of the sampling times, none yielded at least 157 daily cycles while also recovering the same 66 transcripts that earlier research had identified as rhythmic.

The team also found 109 genes with a tidal pattern. That number was no higher than chance alone would produce.

In fruit flies and mammals, CLOCK teams up with a partner protein to turn on clock genes such as period.

The proteins those genes produce then dial back CLOCK and its partner, and the cycle starts again.

No genome exists yet for this mussel. So the team compared three related deep-sea mussels and found two stretches of DNA, just upstream of period, that were nearly identical across species.

The researchers copied those stretches from B. azoricus and tested them in fruit fly cells that lack their own clock parts.

The mussel’s CLOCK and BMAL proteins increased the activity of a test gene controlled by one of those DNA segments.

Industry observers note that A protein called CRY2 shut the signal down, and more CRY2 meant a stronger effect. The mussel’s PER protein had no effect on its own.

Recent findings suggest that added alongside CRY2, though, PER made the shut-off stronger and helped CRY2 build up inside the cell’s nucleus. A third protein, TIM, canceled PER’s effect.

The PER result matters because the period gene in these mussels rises and falls on a roughly tidal schedule.

The researchers suggest the balance between PER and CRY2 could switch the clock between tidal and daily timing.

The deep sea is one of the least explored ecosystems on Earth, and looks for deep-sea mining are putting it under pressure.

Kristin Tessmar-Raible, who studies biological clocks at the University of Oldenburg and the University of Vienna, led the study with Marjolaine Matabos of Ifremer, France’s national ocean research institute.

“The fact that these ecosystems are mechanistically highly complex and possess timing systems as sophisticated as those at the surface underlines how worthy of protection they are,” Tessmar-Raible and Matabos mentioned.

According to recent reports, “On land, we know that human activities such as light or vibrations disrupt circadian clocks. Deep-sea clocks are very likely just as vulnerable, with significant consequences for organisms and ecosystems.”.

The team noted that mining could affect the timing of deep-sea animals even from a great distance.

A dish of cells doesn’t capture everything happening inside a whole mussel at a vent.

The team also detected RNA from the period gene in mussel tissue, while levels in the cultured cells were below what the test could detect.

Either the cells with a tidal rhythm didn’t survive in culture, or conditions in the dish turned off whatever drives the tidal pattern of period, the researchers wrote.

The next question is whether a mussel runs one clock that switches between tides and days, or keeps separate groups of cells that each follow one rhythm. The researchers wrote that their results fit either idea.

Genome studies and work locating the clock proteins inside mussel tissue could help tell those two ideas apart, the team wrote.

The full study was published in the journal EMBO Reports.

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

Industry observers note that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

According to recent reports, but at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

The Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and introduced a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and update climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

But as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she claims. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

Industry observers note that courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

In a recent development, the Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, notes Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

Since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

“When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” says Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

In 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, says Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

University of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

According to recent reports, the effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

“When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin says. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” states Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

Recent findings suggest that but the thing that really stood out, Young notes, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

So, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Industry observers note that larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

Sources indicate that after the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences confirmed a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed aims to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

Industry observers note that “Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” indicates Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

While private funding can be a lifeline, Young states, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

It has been revealed that in 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would matter one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

It has been revealed that but in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

Sources indicate that “Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

In a recent development, in July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

The loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary says. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a new group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

Vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. Currently, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

When the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

While the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell says. It plans to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” says Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

Sources indicate that “I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” states Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Sources indicate that although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm notes. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

In April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp says. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” claims environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a upcoming set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp says.

Sources indicate that the American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” notes Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones notes. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

The Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

“It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” claims Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

In a recent development, climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” says Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

In a recent development, in February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a new website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis says.

Sources indicate that nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

“We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is crucial,” Janis says. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

It has been revealed that at the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, claims colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis claims, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

In a recent development, even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining fresh ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” says Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

Sources indicate that to Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. Latest bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she indicates, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

It has been revealed that powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

It has been revealed that janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

However, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

At the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a fresh science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” says Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

In a recent development, they have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

“If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey says. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.
