The Sans HEPA 13 air purifier offers quiet operation, whole-home purification, and smart features. This unit runs at only 25 decibels on the lowest fan setting, and I could hardly tell that it was on, even when standing next to the unit.

The air purifier is best used for whole-home use, as it purifies spaces up to 1,854 square feet. The internal sensors monitor and show you the air quality index in real time, and the reading is visible on the touch display. I’m able to view PM2.5, which is particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller, such as dust, smoke, pollen, and pet dander, as well as PM10, which are slightly larger particles up to 10 microns, like coarser dust and mold spores.

This unit pairs a medical-grade HEPA 13 filter with a pre-filter, activated carbon filter, and UV-C light to capture 99.9 percent of particles. This might be overkill for general household use, but I’ve appreciated the multi-stage approach. The only downside I’ve come across is that overall cost will likely be higher, considering the Sans recommends replacing the filter every three months.

Industry observers note that there is no shortage of air purifiers on the market, and many of them use a lot of the same tech to achieve better air quality. We’re often testing many different models to find the top recommendations. Ahead are some that haven’t made it to this roundup, but are still worth considering.

It has been revealed that rabbit Air A3 Air Purifier: This air purifier uses a six-stage filtration system to rid your home of smoke, dander, odors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and germs. The lowest fan setting clocks in around 20 decibels, which is extremely quiet, so you can run this model daily without being disturbed. The build is relatively bulky so it’s not the easiest to tuck into a corner and out of the way, and the $760 price tag is pretty steep.

GermGuardian AirSafe+ XL: This model is shaped like our best portable pick above, and comes with a lot of the same features as the other GermGuardian we recommend, and it has a companion app for tracking air quality metrics. That remarked, the app doesn’t specify what type or size particulate matter the sensor is measuring, so it’s hard to tell what common allergens are actually floating around your home.

Air purifiers vary in filtration range, so it's vital to first consider your room size before buying. To find a model that accommodates your space, the EPA recommends that you first multiply the length and width of the area where you intend to operate the air purifier to calculate the square footage.

Most air purifiers have a maximum coverage area listed, so just compare to your calculations to find an air purifier that is the best fit for your home.

Recent findings suggest that if you have an open floor plan or high ceilings, opt for an air purifier with more coverage. You should also place the air purifier in the room you use most regularly, and make sure it’s in an area where the airflow isn’t obstructed.

The filter system of your air purifier might differ depending on the model and issue you're trying to target such as allergy relief, odor elimination, or germ protection. You’ll often see three-stage filtration (or four-, five-, or six-stage), which includes all three of the filter types detailed below.

Pre-filters are typically the first line of defense in an air purifier and trap larger particles like dust, hair, and fur, which helps extend the lifespan of the main filter and improves the overall efficiency of the unit.

All of our selections on this list involve a multi-step filtration system to target a majority of common pollutants and allergens in your household.

Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with NYU Langone Health, recommends selecting an air purifier that comes with a HEPA filter. “Make sure it's a HEPA air purifier since these filter down to 0.3 microns and have a robust amount of studies done showing their efficacy.” HEPA filters remove at least 99.97 percent of airborne particles like dust, bacteria, and pollen, and are the gold standard for air purification.

It has been revealed that activated carbon filters are more porous and help get rid of gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are commonly found in household items like surface cleaners and candles. These filters absorb molecules onto carbon and are best used in environments with strong odors or smoke.

With laundry machines, dishwashers, and fans all emitting their own noise, adding another loud appliance into the mix could be overkill, especially since air purifiers are meant to run the entire day.

Look for models that range from 10 to 30 decibels. A whisper is around 30 decibels, so expect air purifiers in this noise range to be almost virtually silent.

Recent findings suggest that “Air purifiers need to be kept clean, and filters should be changed every six months,” Parikh claims. Since air purifier filters are designed to collect and trap different-sized particles, contaminants, and hair, they get gunky pretty easily. This buildup could even reduce the efficiency and the air quality of the purifier if not cleaned often enough. Most air purifiers come with reusable filters, so just rinse them off in between replacements.

App compatibility, savvy control panels, remotes, check filter indicators, and variable settings are beneficial features that make it easier to use your air purifier. If you want to monitor the air quality levels in your home or keep tabs on filter life, look for an air purifier that pairs with an app. If you’re easily overstimulated by loud noises, consider an air purifier that has different modes for adjusting the speed of the internal fan.

Sources indicate that air purifiers use a fan to draw air into the unit, then pass it through a series of filters to remove particles and contaminants. Mentioned filters vary in effectiveness and normally target a specific concern like odors, smoke, and viruses. Once the air has passed through the fan and all of the appropriate filters, it is recirculated back into the room for a cleaner and healthier environment.

Industry observers note that “Air purifiers filter out pollutants, improve air quality, remove infectious agents and pollen,” states Parikh. “They limit your level of exposure and reduce lung damage and flare-ups of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, and heart complications.”.

In a recent development, “It can affect everyone’s health by causing inflammation and lung damage over time that may be either reversible or irreversible,” Parikh claims. “It is especially dangerous for those with underlying heart disease, lung disease, pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals.”.

These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.
  • Sources indicate that A bigger animal comes with bigger parts.
  • In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.

Sources indicate that A bigger animal comes with bigger parts. A significant dog has a big head, big paws, and a big tail, and the same goes for nearly every creature biologists have measured.

In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.

Their antennae come in the same sizes as the antennae of the much smaller workers, and the colony’s own chemical signals help shape how big each antenna grows.

According to recent reports, A graduate student spotted it by accident under a microscope. Erica Vong, a researcher in Rajendhran Rajakumar’s lab at the University of Ottawa, showed him the antennae of two ants, and the smaller antenna belonged to the soldier.

“Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae,” remarked Rajakumar, an associate professor in the university’s Department of Biology.

The ants belong to Pheidole, the significant-headed ants. Each colony has two kinds of worker: small minors and much larger soldiers whose heads are about twice as wide.

Soldiers defend the nest and mill seeds, and workers do most of the rest.

Rajakumar’s team measured 100 workers and 100 soldiers of one Florida species, Pheidole dentata. For body size they used the width of the thorax just behind the head.

For the antenna they used its first segment, the long stalk that gives an ant’s antenna its elbow shape.

It has been revealed that soldiers had wider bodies and far wider heads, as expected. Their antenna stalks, though, were the same length on average as the workers’, and the whole antenna followed the same pattern.

The two castes’ measurements overlapped so completely that the team couldn’t tell them apart.

Recent findings suggest that within each caste the old rule still held. A bigger worker had a bigger antenna than a smaller worker, and the same was true among soldiers.

Pooled together, the numbers showed no link between antenna and body at all, and the trend only reappeared once the castes were split apart.

Queens were the exception, with larger bodies and larger antennae than either worker caste.

To see whether one species was a fluke, the team pulled published measurements for 565 Pheidole species from the Americas.

Across the 565 species, soldiers and workers often had antenna stalks of similar length, even though soldiers consistently had wider heads.

Recent findings suggest that for each species, Rajakumar’s team divided the soldier’s antenna stalk by the worker’s. The most common answer was one, meaning no difference at all, with some species a little above and some a little below.

The same calculation for head width most often came out at 2 to 1, and no species came in under 1.4 to 1.

The team then measured ants from 14 other genera in three subfamilies, using live colonies, specimens from the Cornell University Insect Collection, and photographs from an online ant database.

In species with no soldier caste, and in most that evolved one on their own, antennae grew with the body as usual.

Recent findings suggest that the one exception was a turtle ant, Cephalotes varians, a close relative of Pheidole. The authors suggest the decoupling first appeared in the common ancestor the two groups share.

Whether a Pheidole larva becomes a worker or a soldier depends on how well it eats. A well-fed larva ends up with more juvenile hormone, and a high enough level turns it into a soldier.

Adult soldiers give off a pheromone that pushes the other way, so a colony with plenty of soldiers makes fewer latest ones.

The team tested both signals on larvae from lab colonies collected in Gainesville, Florida, and kept at 77°F (25°C) on a diet of mealworms and crickets.

They dabbed some larvae with a synthetic version of the hormone and raised each one with either two adult workers or two adult soldiers, starting with 40 larvae per condition.

The larvae were about a twentieth of an inch (1 to 1.5 millimeters) long, young enough that either fate was still open.

Hormone-treated larvae raised by workers became soldiers with a normal spread of antenna sizes.

Recent findings suggest that larvae raised by soldiers without the hormone became workers smaller than any found in a natural colony, with antennae to match. The team calls them nanoworkers.

“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” Rajakumar said.

“They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”.

Larvae that had already passed the point of no return toward becoming soldiers gave the stranger result.

Raised by soldiers, they emerged with soldier-sized heads on worker-sized bodies, and with antenna stalks shorter than those of the smallest natural workers. The team calls these nanosoldiers.

A developing soldier briefly grows a stub of a wing that never becomes a wing, and that stub acts as a signaling center that helps set the soldier’s significant head.

When the team switched off a gene that drives that stub, the larvae grew into smaller ants with smaller heads. Their antennae came out at nearly one size, with almost none of the usual spread.

The team has not found a nanoworker or a nanosoldier in the wild. The authors suspect selection weeds them out.

A soldier’s head on a worker’s body may not be properly supported, and an antenna that small may carry too few sensory hairs to do its job.

The authors also allow that the hidden potential could be a side effect of selection on something else, and the question of which is open.

An ant’s antennae are its main contact with the world. They pick up trail and alarm pheromones, touch, heat, humidity, and vibration, and ants use them to tell nestmates from strangers.

In a recent development, the elbow stalk matters too, because an ant swings it to aim the sensitive tip at whatever it is exploring. The stalk’s length sets where that elbow sits, which affects how an ant probes and follows a trail.

A longer antenna carries more sensory hairs, and earlier work found that how an ant responds to an intruder depends on how many of those hairs it has.

So a colony whose members span a range of antenna sizes may span a range of sensitivities as well.

According to recent reports, rajakumar’s team offers one explanation for why the two castes share a range. When a Pheidole colony runs short of workers, its soldiers take on worker jobs, including caring for young.

Soldiers with the same spread of antenna sizes as workers may make that switch more easily. Once the next generation restores the balance, they can go back to defense.

“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Rajakumar mentioned.

“In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”.

The authors wrote that the adaptive role of the decoupling is still unclear, and the job-switching idea is a hypothesis they haven’t tested.

Their hormone and pheromone experiments used one species, Pheidole dentata.

Roughly half the treated larvae died before reaching adulthood, which the authors attribute to raising each larva with only two adults instead of a full colony.

Antenna length was measured, not the sensory hairs on it, so whether a soldier’s small antenna senses what a worker’s does is still an open question.

The evolutionary story also rests on a single turtle ant species. And 59 Pheidole species were left out of the genus-wide count because one caste or the other had no published measurement.

Checking the relatives is the next step the authors name.

If antennae turn out to be decoupled across the turtle ants and a third genus, Procryptocerus, the pattern would date back to the ancestor of all three.

Until someone measures those ants, the origin stays a hypothesis.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Tech Report: Why are the spiral arms of this galaxy glowing?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.
  • A few bright white stars catch the eye first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.

Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.

A few bright white stars catch the eye first. Behind them, reddish clouds wind around a golden center, tracing the arms of a galaxy about 45 million light-years away.

The James Webb Space Telescope collected the data for this portrait in just 17 minutes of total exposure time.

What makes the image worth a longer look is how much is happening inside those arms.

The bright knots scattered along them show where young stars are already changing the clouds they formed from.

Elsewhere in the same galaxy, a massive star exploded in 2023, returning material to the space between stars.

The large white stars with long, sharp spikes belong to our own Milky Way.

They lie between Earth and NGC 2283 and appear in the picture because they happen to sit along Webb’s line of sight.

In a recent development, their spikes come from the way light bends around parts of the telescope. Once you look past them, the galaxy’s shape is easier to pick out.

Two loosely wound arms curve away from an elongated band of stars that crosses the center.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers call that central structure a bar. Our own galaxy has one, too, but we observe the Milky Way from inside its disk.

Webb sees NGC 2283 almost face-on, giving us a clear view of how its bar and arms fit together.

Webb built this view from six exposures taken through different infrared filters.

Its Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument recorded different parts of the light coming from the same patch of sky.

Industry observers note that combining those observations lets astronomers see several things at once. Some filters pick up light from stars or from clouds of hydrogen energized by young stars.

Others detect the glow of carbon-rich molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are also found in soot on Earth.

Image processors assign visible colors to those infrared measurements.

The result lets us follow details that would otherwise be invisible to our eyes, including the uneven distribution of gas and dust along the arms.

According to recent reports, the spiral arms look almost continuous from a distance. Look closer and they break up into bright clumps, wisps, and darker gaps.

The brightest knots include dense clouds of gas lit up by young stars.

A star begins forming when part of a cold cloud becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity. As material falls inward, the growing star heats up.

Some of the most massive young stars release enough ultraviolet light to energize the hydrogen around them, making the surrounding gas glow.

That glow gives astronomers a way to find places where star formation has happened recently.

In NGC 2283, the glowing clouds and young clusters make it possible to trace the arms even where dust hides some of the stars.

On January 28, 2023, astronomers discovered a supernova in NGC 2283.

Known as SN 2023AXU, it was a Type II supernova, the kind that can occur when a massive star runs out of fuel in its core.

Recent findings suggest that once the core can no longer support itself against gravity, it collapses. The resulting explosion throws the star’s outer layers into space.

Over time, material from explosions like this can mix with surrounding gas and become part of clouds that form latest stars.

That process changes the ingredients available to later generations.

Elements such as oxygen and sodium can travel far from the star that released them, then end up in another star or in the material that gathers around it.

NGC 2283 is one of 55 nearby galaxies Webb observed in a program designed to study how stars, gas, and dust interact.

These galaxies are close enough for Webb to distinguish individual star clusters and gas clouds, allowing astronomers to compare conditions from one part of a galaxy to another.

According to recent reports, in this portrait, the spiral arms may be the first thing you notice. The small knots along them are what make the scene worth coming back to.

Each marks a place where young stars are already leaving a visible imprint on the material around them.

How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday.
  • More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.
  • Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:.

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

In a recent development, the outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Recent findings suggest that still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore noted, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

Sources indicate that the group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the latest lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Industry observers note that groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”.

Republican efforts to try again and enact a upcoming congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

It has been revealed that A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of Latest England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

According to recent reports, with over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

In a recent development, under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”.

According to recent reports, the state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year. Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Sources indicate that then last week, the Senate race was upended by a Latest York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

It has been revealed that dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that right now use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#77253. Narwhals helped solve a mystery deep in Greenland’s fjords

Narwhals helped solve a mystery deep in Greenland’s fjords

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sensors carried by six narwhals demonstrated warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.
  • Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.
  • Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sensors carried by six narwhals demonstrated warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.

Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.

Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.

This matters because melting glaciers release freshwater into the North Atlantic. That water can change ocean layers, currents, and climate patterns far beyond Greenland.

Yet many East Greenland fjords are difficult to reach. Sea ice, harsh weather, and long distances often keep research ships away, leaving major gaps in ocean records.

In a recent development, six narwhals have now helped fill some of those gaps in data from fjords. Sensors carried during their normal dives demonstrated warmer Atlantic water reaching deep fjords and glacier fronts far inland.

Scoresby Sound lies on Greenland’s east coast and forms the world’s largest fjord system.

Industry observers note that fjords are long, narrow arms of the sea that reach deep into the land. Narwhals can move through fjord areas that ships rarely reach.

Professor Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen of the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources helped lead the work.

“The narwhals have been in parts of the fjords where very few measurements have been taken before. And there, 300 kilometers from the coast, we find traces of Atlantic water.

“It is completely new that we can show this,” noted Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Local hunters helped capture and tag six narwhals near Scoresby Sound. The tags measured water temperature, salt level, depth, and location for between 85 and 332 days.

Between 2017 and 2020, the animals collected 2,060 ocean profiles.

Each profile recorded water conditions at several depths during a dive, giving the team repeated readings from remote waters that ships rarely sample directly.

Some readings came from more than 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) below the surface.

Professor Susanne Ditlevsen of the University of Copenhagen helped analyze the large collection.

According to recent reports, “Now we suddenly have measurements from places we can use in our models, giving us a much more complete picture of the ocean. It is absolutely fantastic to use the animals in this way,” said Professor Ditlevsen.

East Greenland has cold Polar Water near the surface and warmer, saltier Atlantic water below it. Salinity simply means the amount of salt in water.

The team combined the narwhal readings with more than 2,200 older profiles from the World Ocean Database.

It then built a model, which is a math tool that finds patterns in large amounts of data.

“We used the two large datasets to build a robust model showing how temperature, salinity and depth are related,” explained Professor Ditlevsen.

“The models show that the layer consisting of Atlantic water has become thicker, while the upper layer of Polar Water has become thinner,” she added.

The results point to a stronger Atlantic influence in the region.

The Blosseville Basin warmed over the study period, with summer records showing warming in both the colder Polar Water and the warmer Atlantic water.

In a recent development, the shape of the seafloor controls where deep water can travel. Shallow ridges may block it, while deep channels can carry it toward glaciers.

Atlantic water became the main water type below about 820 feet (250 meters) in the Blosseville Basin.

It also crossed an underwater ridge and moved into the remote inner parts of Scoresby Sound.

The warmer water reached glacier basins about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from the coast.

Glaciers in deep basins faced warmer and saltier water than glaciers along the shallower Blosseville Coast.

Industry observers note that this shows why fjord depth matters. A glacier can sit far inland and still receive Atlantic water when a deep route connects it to the open sea.

Industry observers note that the team compared ocean conditions with the amount of ice that broke away from glaciers. This process is called iceberg discharge.

Where water at 1,310 feet (400 meters) was warmer and saltier, icebergs accounted for a larger share of the glaciers’ total summer ice loss.

“This is the water that helps melt the glaciers. We show how the warm water can contribute to accelerating the rate at which glaciers lose ice,” noted Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Ocean heat can reach the ice from below, but the results do not show that warm water caused every change in glacier loss.

Air temperature, surface melting, seafloor shape, and local glacier conditions also matter, so the pattern does not point to one simple cause.

Only six narwhals carried sensors, and the animals chose their own routes.

Because narwhals prefer cold water, they may have spent less time in the warmer Atlantic layer.

The older ocean records were also uneven. Few measurements came from some fjords before 2010, so long-term changes inside Scoresby Sound remain difficult to judge.

The tags were not recovered after use. The team could not check them again for small changes in accuracy, especially in the salt readings.

Winter findings need extra care because narwhals provided most of the recent winter measurements. Their routes may not represent the whole region.

Climate models use real measurements to estimate how Earth may change.

Better ocean records can improve estimates of future glacier melt in Greenland, a point that Professor Ditlevsen connected to the larger climate question.

“In the large climate models used to predict future climate change, glacier melt plays a major role. That is why it is crucial that we improve our understanding of it, particularly because Greenland contains so much ice.”.

Sources indicate that the latest data can strengthen future climate estimates. Narwhals cannot replace ships, satellites, or long-term ocean stations, but they can reach waters that people struggle to measure.

Their dives revealed a clear route for warm Atlantic water into remote fjords.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics.
  • Significant thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers.
  • Sources indicate that staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with fresh parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

Industry observers note that science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

Significant thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” notes senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a latest appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

Sources indicate that staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with fresh parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús states. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Organization | $29.99.

It has been revealed that adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

According to recent reports, senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen notes. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Industry observers note that senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, upcoming mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

According to recent reports, for the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Sources indicate that conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover claims. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

Riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”.

Latest Update: The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

📅 12 Jun 2020 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely.
  • Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed its listed max output to see how well it could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

According to recent reports, bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts (with 3,900-watt startup power) and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

It has been revealed that the Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

It has been revealed that A fresh and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

It has been revealed that the Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Industry observers note that performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that this power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

In a recent development, what is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

One of the standout features of Bluetti’s Apex 200 is a maximum solar input of up to 3,000 watts. You rarely find that much input power for a station of this size. There are two sets of DC inputs for this: low-voltage XT60 input (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 input (up to 2,000 watts). If you have the panels and enough perfect direct sunlight to achieve this full potential, you could fully charge this station in less than two hours using the sun’s rays.

Beyond that, the Apex 200 is a fairly robust power station, with 3,200 watts of continuous power. (It says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery.) I ran my refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and when I tested it for battery efficiency, I estimated it at about 90 percent, which is very good for a power station. There’s also a 120-volt 30-amp output if you wanted to run a few circuits in your home by hooking up to a manual transfer switch. Just keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

The 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity isn't huge—at least not for home backup—but you can expand it by adding up to six additional batteries. That could add up to over 33 kilowatt-hours if you use the largest batteries Bluetti offers, the B500K. That’s massive.

It has been revealed that even with all this power, the Apex 200 is still a fairly portable station. Weighing 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. So, when you’re not using it for home backup, it’s perfect for taking on a long outdoor trip or for powering an RV when a site hookup is not available.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

Industry observers note that this is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

In a recent development, the unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

It has been revealed that the S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

In a recent development, the next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

In a recent development, during our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and upcoming outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

Recent findings suggest that we loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

Sources indicate that the mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

It has been revealed that though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In a recent development, in testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

According to recent reports, recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

Recent findings suggest that the Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the crucial information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

Sources indicate that all of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via WiFi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge for a full eight months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

Recent findings suggest that A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you blueprint to plug into it.

Recent findings suggest that some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds when you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

According to recent reports, A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048-watt-hour capacity and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that the usable watt-hours are not the same as the watt-hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

It has been revealed that these days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Midsize models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Sources indicate that portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large-capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Industry observers note that portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Recent findings suggest that often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

Recent findings suggest that how much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

Recent findings suggest that that depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

According to recent reports, some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you blueprint on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

#77250. Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A new map offers surprises

Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A new map offers surprises

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.
  • Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.
  • A upcoming global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A upcoming global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

Sources indicate that across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

Europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

In the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

Recent findings suggest that global averages hide massive differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

Freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he said.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant stated.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles revealed the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

The hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

It has been revealed that “What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he stated.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into plans explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

Sources indicate that the maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

Asked which places he would look at first, Brabant remarked threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he mentioned.

What would help most right now, he stated, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
